summary:
We developed Project Astryn, an interactive browser-based outpost management simulation designed for students ages 7–12. Built with a zero-install, no-login web architecture powered by a high-speed Rust/WebAssembly simulation engine, the app puts young learners in the commander’s seat of a lunar or Martian habitat.

The game directly addresses the challenge by turning deep-space engineering constraints into tangible, real time trade offs. Rather than presenting passive facts, players must actively balance finite power generation, oxygen life support, food production, and radiation shielding where upgrading one module increases resource strain across the base. By integrating real solar flare and space weather datasets from NASA’s DONKI database alongside biological constraints informed by OSDR, dynamic events like dust storms and radiation spikes force players to make high-stakes choices and immediately observe the consequences.

This project is important because space education often oversimplifies mission mechanics or hides them behind intimidating technical jargon. By bridging authentic NASA science with intuitive base building gameplay, our simulator empowers the next generation of explorers to develop systems thinking skills and truly understand what it takes to sustain human life beyond Earth.

MARS OPS: THE LAST OUTPOST — Project Submission

What does it do / How does it work?

MARS OPS: THE LAST OUTPOST is a browser-based 3D voxel survival simulator where players command a human research outpost on Mars. Instead of passive quizzes or dashboards, it teaches real aerospace engineering through hands-on gameplay.

Players control a voxel astronaut across six functional zones modeled after real NASA infrastructure — a Habitat Hub with an ECLSS life-support console, a Power Station with sun-tracking solar arrays, a Greenhouse with hydroponic trays, a Science Lab with a MOXIE oxygen processor, a Communications Station, and a Rover Pad.

A real-time simulation engine runs every frame, computing interdependent resource dynamics:

  • Power follows a physically accurate diurnal solar zenith curve, attenuated by dust storms
  • Oxygen is produced via MOXIE solid-oxide CO₂ electrolysis — only when battery > 5%
  • Water runs a closed-loop recycler at 80–98% efficiency, subject to membrane failures
  • Temperature drops to −40°C in a blackout, triggering hypothermia
  • Radiation spikes during solar storms; players build sintered regolith berms to shield the crew
  • Crew Health degrades when any vital crosses a critical threshold

A 7-mission campaign guides players from outpost orientation through inverter repair, crater ice mining, water recycling, greenhouse cultivation, surviving a Class-5 dust storm, and autonomous long-term survival. Every mission ends with a NASA Flight Heritage Debrief linking gameplay to real NASA programs and technical documentation.

What benefits does it have?

  • Active learning: Players diagnose a burned inverter, mine subsurface ice, calibrate an oxygen electrolyzer, and flush a water membrane — mirroring real astronaut maintenance procedures rather than reading about them.
  • Scientifically grounded: Solar curves, thermal differentials, kWh battery math, and radiation shielding decay all use physically motivated equations — not arbitrary numbers.
  • Universally accessible: Runs in any web browser, no downloads required. Supports both keyboard/mouse and mobile touch controls. Autosaves every 30 seconds.
  • Genuinely engaging: 3D isometric voxel world, dynamic day/night lighting, procedural audio, and an immersive sci-fi HUD keep players immersed long enough for the science to sink in.

What is the intended impact?

To make real aerospace engineering — ECLSS, ISRU, photovoltaics, thermal management — tangible and exciting for learners aged 10–18, before they ever reach a university course. By experiencing cascading system failures firsthand (a dust storm cuts solar power → battery drains → MOXIE shuts off → oxygen drops → crew health falls), players build genuine systems-thinking skills and leave with real NASA references to follow up on.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Technology

Role

TypeScript

Entire codebase — type-safe game architecture

React 19

HUD, modals, menus, and all overlay UI

Three.js

3D orthographic isometric renderer — procedural voxel geometry, PCF shadows, dynamic lighting, fog, particle systems

Zustand

Reactive state store driving both simulation and UI

Vite 8

Build tooling and development server

Web Audio API

100% procedural soundscape — Martian wind, spacesuit breathing, generator hum, alarms, footsteps. Zero audio files.

LocalStorage

30-second autosave and manual save slots

Git / GitHub

Version control

No specialized hardware required — runs on any modern browser, including school Chromebooks.

How is your project creative?

  1. Zero external assets: Every building, terrain feature, the astronaut, the rover, and the entire outpost are built entirely from Three.js geometry primitives in code. No 3D model files, no texture images, no audio files — everything is synthesized at runtime.
  2. Emergent cascading failures: Resources aren't isolated bars. A dust storm triggers a chain: reduced solar → faster battery drain → MOXIE offline → oxygen drops → temperature plunges → crew health collapses. Players must think like real flight controllers.
  3. Multi-step diagnostic repairs: Fixing the inverter means isolating bus breakers, replacing a burned IGBT module, and calibrating MPPT firmware. Repairing MOXIE means venting CO lines, replacing a Yttria-Stabilized Zirconia electrolyzer core, and preheating to 800°C — sequences modeled on real astronaut maintenance procedures.
  4. Fully procedural audio: The entire Martian soundscape — howling wind that intensifies during storms, rhythmic spacesuit breathing, metallic footsteps, spark welders, escalating alarms — is synthesized live using Web Audio API oscillators and filters. Not a single audio file is loaded.
  5. NASA debrief system: Completing each mission unlocks an educational card that connects the gameplay action to a real NASA program (MOXIE on Perseverance, ISS ECLSS, NASA Veggie, Deep Space Network) with a direct link to official NASA documentation.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Accuracy vs. playability: A full Martian Sol plays out in ~8 real minutes — fast enough to be engaging, slow enough to observe and respond. All physics models are simplified but directionally correct.
  • Cognitive scaffolding: Each mission introduces one system at a time. By Mission 7, players manage everything simultaneously — but they've built up to it gradually.
  • Performance on low-end hardware: The voxel art style was a deliberate choice. Shadow resolution, pixel ratio, fog, and particle counts were tuned for smooth 60 FPS on integrated GPUs.
  • Respect for player time: Autosave every 30 seconds ensures no progress is lost to a classroom bell or accidental tab close.
  • Real-world grounding: Every debrief cites actual NASA missions, instruments, and public technical reports — leaving players with real breadcrumbs into aerospace engineering.
